ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Education to all by 2003 
*161.   SHRI K. NATWAR SINGH: 
DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY:† 
Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether the Minister has given an assurance that all the children would 
be provided schooling by 2003;  
(b) if so, what steps Government propose to take to implement this 
assurance; and 
(c) what steps both the Centre and States have taken together, to achieve 
this   objective? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (DR. MURLI 
MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) to (c) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (c) The Government has taken necessary steps to amend the 
Constitution to make free and compulsory education a fundamental right for 
all children in the age group 6—14. In addition to these steps for amendment 
of the Constitution, the Government has also launched Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan 
(SSA) in partnership with the States with the objective of getting all children 
in this age group into schools, Education Guarantee Scheme centres or back 
to school camps by the academic year 2003. The progr-mn.e is being 
implemented through State Level Societies, with the funding being shared 
between the Central Government and the State Government in the ratio of 
85:15 in the Ninth Plan, 75:25 in the Tenth Plan and 50:50 thereafter. 
The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Dr. T. 
Subbarami Reddy. 

RAJYA SABHA [29 November, 2002] 
Under the programme District Elementary Education Plans (DEEP) are 
prepared according to the needs identified and the stipulated guidelines. 
These Plans are then approved by the Project Approval Board. The District 
Primary Education Programme (DPEP) in 273 districts, Lok Jumbish Programme 
(LJP) in 13 districts and Shiksha Karmi Programme (SKP) in 31 districts are 
also being implemented within the SSA framework. During the current financial 
year till 25th November 2002, the total outlay approved under SSA including 
DPEP, LJP and SKP components, is Rs. 4335.66 crores. DEEPs for 201 districts 
with an anticipated outlay of Rs. 700 crores for the remaining period of the 
financial year are currently being appraised. 
DR. T. SUBBARAMIREDDY: Madam, I would like to know from the hon. 
Minister whether, in the recent UNESCO Conference on the Literacy Day, in 
the presence of the hon. Vice-President, he has committed that primary 
education would be made available for all the children in the country by 2003. 
At the same time, it has been mentioned in a newspaper report that the 
Government of India has committed that primary education would be made 
available for all children by 2005. So, there are two different dates. Also, there 
is a contradiction in the figures. One version says that it is 63 million children 
and the other version puts it at 80 million children who are, actually, to be 
educated. So, firstly, I would like to be enlightened as to which is the correct 
figure. 
The second point is that the hon. Minister is committed to provide primary 
education for all children by 2003, but we are already in 2002. So, what is 
going to happen to the set target and what action his Ministry has taken so 
far? 
The third point is, the hon. Minister has mentioned in his reply that up to 
November 25,2002, he has approved Rs. 4,335.66 crores. I would like to know 
from the hon. Minister as to what is the total money required to achieve the 
goal of providing primary education to all children in the country—may be, 
by 2003 or 2005 or any time. So far, you have approved only Rs. 4,335 crores. 
What is the balance amount required to achieve the goal? What is the plan of 
the Government to provide the balance amount? 
DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI: Madam, it is a very long question. 
The first point is, it must be very clear to this august House that the goal 
set by the Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan is to carry all the children, between 
2 

[29 November, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
6—14 age group, to school system from the academic session 2003 and 
complete their education by the end of the academic session 2010. This is an 
advancement and improvement over the international goal which has set it as 
2015. But the Government of India has set this goal as 2010. Now, there should 
be no doubt about it—the year set is 2003, not 2005. 
The second point is, there are about 18 crore students in the age group of 
6—14 years. Out of it, only about 3.5 crores are out of the mainstream. So, 
that number is clear. Statistics are available with us. So far as the money point 
is concerned, the Government of India and the State Governments have made 
a commitment to complete this scheme on a mutually-sharing basis. In the first 
phase, there would be a sharing in the ratio of 85:15; in the second phase, in 
the ratio of 75:25; and in the third phase, in the ratio of 50:50. So, whatever 
money is required for it, would be shared like this. It is estimated that roughly 
20 million dollars would be used for it, and the amount would be shared by 
the Central Government and the State Governments. If there are some other 
sources of funding, we would use them also. So, there is no difficulty in 
arranging the money. So, far as the progress in the work i: concerned, up till 
now, we have spent more than Rs. 4,600 crores. The schemes for other States, 
from which the projects have now come, are in the pipeline. I think, by the 
end of December, we would be completing an investment of Rs. 5000 crores. 
DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: Madam, my second supplementary is this. 
In spite of Government's efforts the dropout rate is increasing in the Central 
Schools. So, there is a need for providing the mid-day meal in schools. Is it a 
fact that the hon. Supreme Court has given a ruling that cooked mid-day meal 
should compulsorily be provided in schools? If the mid-day meal is not 
provided in the schools by the State Governments, the Central Government 
should stop providing funds to them. So, what action is the Government 
going to take in this regard? As per the directions of the hon. Supreme Court, 
are you going to make this mid-day meal scheme compulsory in the schools 
all over India? 
THE DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: Yesterday, Shabana Azmiji had also raised this 
issue in a Special Mention. 
DR. MURLIMANOHAR JOSHI: Madam, as far as the mid-day mp1 scheme 
is concerned, the Government of India provides cereals and transportation 
charges. We are also trying to build up the scheme through which the cooked 
meal is provided to children in all the schools. About eight States have 
already implemented this scheme. We are trying to see that other States also 
start providing cooked mid-day meal in the schools. It has its own problems.

(b) if so, whether Government have made vocational education a focus

provide job oriented education at school level. The University Grants 
Commission also has a programme, namely, Career Orientation Scheme under

corporate houses through Chamber of Indian Industries (CII), etc. for making 
the education job oriented. 
(c) and (d) Since School Education is primarily the responsibility of State 
Governments, various issues involved in the Vocationalisation of Secondary 
Education, including involvement of industries and corporate houses were 
discussed at the Education Secretaries Conference held in August 2002. The 
State Governments have by and large supported the scheme of 
Vocationalisation of Education and the idea of developing linkages of vocational 
programmes with the industry for its success.

MISS MABEL REBELLO: 
Will the Minister YOUTH AFFAIRS AND SPORTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news report 
captioned, "Manchester drug disgrace-Government knew there was suspect in 
team", which appeared in the Indian Express dated the 3rd September, 2002; 
†The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shri B. J. 
Panda. 
16 

[29 November, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) whether it is a fact that the Indian weight-lifter, who had won the gold 
medat was tested positive shortly before he left India; and 
(c) if so, how he was cleared for the games and what are the reasons for 
the lapse? 
THE MINISTER OF YOUTH AFFAIRS AND SPORTS (SHRI VIKRAM 
VERMA): (a) to (c) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir. The news report has been gone through, it is, however, denied 
that the Government had been aware that there was any drug suspect in the 
team. A rejoinder to this news report was issued by the Sports Authority of 
India (SAI), vide letter dated 3.9.2002 addressed to the Editor, Indian Express, 
clarifying that the news report, imputing knowledge to the Government in this 
regard, is misleading and baseless. 
(b) and (c) The news-item relates to Shri Madasamy, weightlifter, who, 
according to the news report, had won a gold medal in Commonwealth Games 
at Manchester, which is factually incorrect. Shri Madasamy had not won any 
gold medal. He had won three silver medals, which were taken back from him 
due to his testing positive for use of 'Nandrolone' during the Commonwealth 
Games. The concerned International Federation has also enforced two years' 
ban on him. Shri Sateesha Rai, another weightlifter, who had won 2 Gold and 
1 bronze medals at these Games, had also tested pc^itive for use of'Strychnine', 
a banned substance, due to which, his medals were taken back and a six 
months' ban and a USD 1000 fine was imposed on him by the concerned 
International Federation. 
Sports Authority of India (SAI) has instituted a one-man Inquiry Committee 
to probe these incidents. The Committee had submitted its report, on 
examination whereof, it was found that the Committee had not inquired into 
certain vital aspects of these incidents. Director General, Sports Authority of 
India has, accordingly, been asked to fiirther inquire into these aspects. The 
final report is yet to be received. However, pending fmal outcome of tfie 
inquiry, following actions have been taken in this matter :— 
(a) The SAI Coach, Shri K. Manilal, who was attached with the National 
coaching camp for weightlifting was placed under suspension. 
(b) The Chief Coach of the weightlifting camp, Shri Tamil Selvan, who  
belonged to Railways, was sent back to his parent Department, advising 
them to take action against him. 
17 

RAJYA SABHA [29 November, 2002] 
(c) The Coach, Shri C.S. Shivrama, attached with the weightlifting camp. 
has been sent back to the Kamataka Government which has been 
asked to take action against him. 
(d) Shri Durgalal Meena, Lab Technician has been removed from the 
contractual service for negligence of duty. 
(e) Both these players, who tested positive for dope during Commonweahh 
Games-2002, have been debarred from entering the SAI campus for 
any training or other activities. 
Further action will be taken on the basis of the final outcome of the  
inquiry.

Bamboo flowering 
*165. DR. ARUN KUMAR SARMA: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) the phenomenal causes of bamboo flowering and its repeatability, 
predictions, implications, including famine, based on past experience; 
(b) what is the probable period of bamboo flowering, action taken by the 
Ministry to face the situation, State-wise; and 
(c) the utility of bamboo seeds, if any, because of enhancing prolificacy 
of rats? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. BAALU); 
(a) The flowering of bamboos normally takes place in a cyclic manner after a 
fixed number of years and the cycle repeats after almost the same interval. 
This phenomenon makes the prospective flowering predictable to a large, 
extent. The flowering is followed by the death of the flowered clumps. The 
flowering can be sporadic (scattered over the locality) or gregarious (all the 
clumps in a locality flowering together). 
The implications are, increase in vulnerability of the area to forest fires due 
to high inflammability of dry bamboo clumps, problems of harvesting and 
marketing of large quantity of bamboo from remote areas and protection of 
tender shoots from grazing after the seeds germinate. 
In Mizoram and some other areas of North Eastern Region, the biggest 
problem is the explosion in rodent population with the seeding which, after 
the seeds germinate, head towards farmlands in the adjoining areas and cause 
damage to crops and foodgrains. Such a chain of events has the potential to 
cause famine. 
26 

[29 November, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
The phenomenon cause of bamboo flowering and death of its clumps 
thereafter is still not clearly known. 
(b) The flowering cycle of bamboos depends on the species of the bamboo 
plant and not the State. In most of the States except Mizoram and some other 
areas of North East, the flowered clumps are harvested immediately after 
flowering and adequate measures are also taken for protection of area against 
fires and grazing. The main area of concern is Mizoram, which has the past 
experience of famine like conditions due to rodent menace. The details of 
flowering of Muli Bamboo (Melocanna baccifera) and Peka Bamboo (Bambusa 
tulda) in Mizoram are as under.

Private Participation in Agriculture Sector 
* 179. SHRl K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: 
SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDYSIRIGIREDDY:' 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that private participation in agricultural extension is 
vital for development of agriculture in the country; 
(b) whether any study has been carried out by the Ministry with regard to 
providing extension services and the willingness to pay for the services; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI AJIT SINGH): (a) Yes, Sir. The 
private participation in agricultural extension is important as it will help 
complement and supplement the public extension system which has weakened 
in several States as a result of financial constraints being experienced by them. 
(b) Yes, Sir. 
(c) Details are annexed as Statement. 
Statement 
Details of the Study on Private Participation in Agriculture Sector 
The acceptability of a network of Agri-Clinics and Agri-Business Centres 
was assessed by the Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) through a 
quick survey entrusted to Agricultural Universities located in Pantnagar 
(Uttaranchal), Pusa (Bihar) and Akola (Maharashtra) andNational Academy of 
Agricultural Research Management, Hyderabad (Andhra Pradesh). The survey 
covered both, farmers, who would be the clients, and agricultural graduates, 
48 

[29 November, 2002] RAA'A SABHA 
who would be the service providers. The survey indicates that farming 
community would welcome such a network and would be willing to pay for 
certain selected services to be rendered by these Clinics/Centres, such as 
services relating to soil and water quality testing, livestock health cover, custom 
hiring of machinery and implements, seed processing and extension consultancy 
services. The response was more positive from progressive farmers and those 
with large/medium holdings. The survey of agriculture graduates also indicated 
that the scheme would be, by and large, welcome provided, it had a provision for 
training in entrepreneurial and business management skills. 
The Department of Agricuhure and Cooperation after wide consultation with -
various stakeholders has brought out a "Policy framework for Agricultural 
Extension (2001)" in conformity with the National Agriculture Policy. The 
provisions including private participation and payment for services are being 
pilot tested under Innovations in Technology Dissemination (ITD) component of 
World Bank funded National Agricultural Technology Project (NATP). It covers 
Seven States namely Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Himachal Pradesh, Jharkhand, 
Maharashtra, Orissa and Punjab with four districts in each. Agricultural 
Technology Management Agencies (ATMAs), as an autonomous organization, 
have been established at the district level representing various stakeholders with 
an objective of working out new institutional arrangements to facilitate 
extension reforms. These efforts are proposed to be operationalized/up-scaled 
during Xth Plan through a new Centrally Sponsored Scheme—Support to State 
Extension Programmes for Extension Reforms,

Study on Ganga Pollution 
1115. SHRI KAILASH JOSHI: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) when was the Ganga Action Plan started; 
(b) what are the details of tortuous attempts made to clean the Gang^ and the 
amount spent so far; 
(c) how many studies were conducted and the rep6rts submitted so far, giving 
the details thereof; 
(d) whether Government have planned one more study for control of pollution 
by an international agency; if so, the details thereof and the amount earmarked 
for the purpose; and 
(e) by when the report is likely to be presented? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. BAALU) 
(a) and (b) The Ganga Action Plan (GAP) has been taken up in two phases. The 
first phase of Ganga Action Plan was started in 1985 with the objective of 
preventing the pollution of river Ganga and to improve its water quality along 
25 towns. The Plan was completed on 31.3.2000 and an amount of Rs. 451.70 
crore has been spent. Against a target capacity of 873 million litres per day 
(mid) planned for treatment of wastewater, a capacity to treat 865 mid has been. 
created. 
The GAP Phase-Il, which covers Ganga and its tributaries viz. Yamuna, Gomti 
115 

RAJYA SABHA [29 November, 2002] 
and Damodar was approved in phases between 1993 and 1996 and is under 
implementation. Out of an approved cost of Rs. 1498.86 crore, an amount of 
Rs. 732.80 crore has been spent and a capacity to treat 724 mid of wastewater 
has been created so far. The GAP Phas e-II is targeted for completion by 
December, 2005. 
(c) A comprehensive evaluation of GAP Phase-I by independent agencies 
(universities and R&D institutions) was undertaken in April, 1995. The 
evaluation report concluded that reduction of discharge of organic matter, a 
necessary first step in restoring the water quality of the river, has been achieved 
to a fair level under GAP Phase-I. Concern was expressed about contamination 
of the river with bacterial pollution and the need to address the same. However, 
it was stated that GAP Phase-I as conceived and implemented is an appropriate 
programme for application to other river basins. The shortcomings of the 
programme have also been brought out in the report and have been taken note 
of for modification in the subsequent programmes. 
On the directions of the Planning Commission, a Cost Benefit Analysis of 
Ganga Action Plan was carried out in 1995-96 by the Harvard Institute of 
International Development, U.K. in collaboration with reputed national institutes, 
the Study demonstrated that: 
(i) inspite of its many shortcomings, the Ganga Action Plan has delivered 
significant benefits to India and there have been improvements in water 
quality (measured in terms of dissolved oxygen and bio-chemical oxygen 
demand) in some places. The polluted stretch of the river violating the 
bathing class standard, which would have been atleast 740 kms. between 
Kannauj and Varanasi without GAP Phase-1 had been reduced to 437 
kms. after completion of GAP Phase-I. 
(ii) both users and non-users have benefited and the result is that the real 
rate of return on GAP Phase-I is well above the 10% required of public 
sector projects. 
(iii) in terms of both the cost involved and the time taken, Ganga Action 
Plan compared favourably with other clean-up programmes undertaken 
In the world for rivers Thames, Rhine and Danube. 
The Central Pollution Control Board, on the directions of the Suprqm«sCourt, 
carried out a detailed inspection of the sewage treatment plants (STPs) set up 
under GAP ;Phase-l in July, 2001. The Inspection Report of the Central Pollution 
Control Board concluded that out of the 35 STPs sanctioned under GAP 
116 

[29 November, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
Phase-I, 32 were commissioned and of these 29 were found flinctioning. The 
report also indicates that adequate ftind allocation for operation and maintenance 
of STPs is not provided, particularly in Bihar and UP. 
(d) and (e) The Japan International Cooperation Agency of the Government 
of Japan has recently agreed to provide technical assistance for taking up a 
development study on 'Water Quality Management Plan for river Ganga'. The 
objective of the study is to (i) formulate the Master Plan for water quality 
management for the Ganga basin concerning liquid waste, and (ii) formulate 
feasibility studies for high priority projects identified in the Master Plan focusing 
on four towns namely, Kanpur, Allahabad, Varanasi and Lucknow. This study is 
different than the three studies mentioned in para (c) above as it aims at 
formulating the remaining works to be taken up over and above those 
implemented/proposed to be implemented under GAP Phase-! and II in the four 
towns in the Ganga Basin. It will take two years to complete the study.

1132. SHRI S.S. CHANDRAN: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT   be pleased to state: 
(a) what is the percentage of literates in backward districts of the country; 
(b) whether Government have any plans to improve this percentage; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT [DR. (SHRIMATI) RITA VERMAj: (a) As per Census 2001 
Report, the literacy rate for all persons in India is 65.38%. The percentage of

129 

RAJYA SABHA [29 November, 2002] 
(b) and (c) The steps being taken to improve the literacy rate are as 
under:— 
(I) A new scheme of Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA) has been started for 
Universalization of Elementary Education in a mission mode with a 
district focus. SSA is to provide useful and relevant Elementary 
Education for all children in the 6—14 age group by 2010. The goals 
are as follows: 
* All children in school, Education Guarantee Scheme Centre, 
Alternate   School, 'Back-to-School' camps by 2003. 
* All children complete five years primary education by 2007. 
* All children complete eight years of schooling by 2010. 
* Focus on elementary education of satisfactory quality with emphasis 
on education for life. 
* Bridge all gender and social gaps at primary stage by 2007 and at 
elementary education level by 2010. 
* Universal retention by 2010. 
National Literacy Mission (MLM) seeks to attain full literacy, i.e. a 
sustainable threshold level of 75 per cent by 2005. It seeks to achieve this 
goal by imparting functional literacy to non-literates in 15^35 year age group. 
Major thrust of the programme is on promotion of literacy among women. In 
the literacy programmes, 60% of the le arners are women and around 60% of 
volunteers also are women and young girls. 
Various facets of literacy related backwardness like low female literacy, 
SC/ST literacy etc. are being addressed through the above-mentioned efforts.

1143. SHRl R.P. GOENKA : Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether h is a fact that a large number of private technical and non-
technical institutes, that have mushroomed across the country, have requested 
for grant of Deemed University status;

(c) the details of guidelines laid down for maintaining objectivity in 
evaluating the private institutes for grant of the required status and the role 
assigned therefor to the UGC and the AICTE? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT [DR. (SHRIMATI) RITA VERMA]: (a) and (b) Various 
institutions have applied for grant of Deemed to be University status. A list 
of such institutions is annexed as statement (See below). Declaration of an 
institution as Deemed University is a statutory process done on fulfillment of 
several requirements under the guidelines. 
(c) Proposals for Deemed University status are examined in consultation 
with UGC and AICTE. UGC and AICTE have laid down the guidelines for 
considering the proposals for declaring an institution as Deemed to be 
University. These guidelines, inler-alia, provide that an institution should 
generally be: 
(i) Engaged in teaching programmes and research in chosen fields of 
specialisation which are innovative and very high academic 
standards at the Master's (or equivalent) and/or research levels. It 
should also have a greater interface with society through extra 
mural, extension and field action related programmes. 
(ii) Making in its areas of specialisation, distinct contribution to the 
objectives of the University education system through innovative 
programmes and on being recognised as a university capable of 
further enriching the university system as well as strengthening 
teaching and research in the institution and particularly in its area 
of specialisation. 
(iii)   Competent to undertake application-oriented programmes in 
emerging areas which are relevant and useful to various 
development sectors and to the society in general. 145 

RAJYA SABHA [29 November. 2002] 
(iv) Institutions should have the necessary viabihty and a management 
capable of contributing to the university ideals and traditions, 
Ordinarily, institutions affiliated to university and which are offering only 
conventional degree programmes leading to BA/B.Com/B.Sc. or MA/M.Com/ 
M.Sc, will not be considered for grant of deemed to be university status. 
However, such institution which is also offering innovative programmes, and 
which has adequate resources, might be considered for recognition as a 
university. Supplementary assistance for innovation may be considered by 
the UGC only in such exceptional cases.  
Institutions which are imparling routine type of instruction to full-time 
students or offering training programmes for in-service personnel, unless of 
high quality, would, generally, not qualify for recognition. 
In selective cases, outstanding research institutions specialising in Social 
Sciences, Sciences and Technology can be considered for research degree 
and highly specialised programmes at the Master's level. 
In case the institution is offering a degree/diploma, in professional 
subject(s), the acacdemic programme(s) should be recognised by the 
concerned statutory authority e.g. All India Council for Technical Education 
(AiCTE), Medical Council of India (MCI). Dental Council of India (DCI), 
Central Council of Homoeopathy (CCH), Indian Nursing Council (INC) etc. 
before it applies for a deemed to be university status under Section 3 of the 
UGC Act. 
This shall, however, not apply to de-novo institutions in the emerging 
areas with the promise of excellence, not yet fulfilling the prescribed guidelines 
of the UGC whose case will be considered for a provisional status for a 
Deemed to be University.

SHRI M. V. RAJASEKHARAN (Kamataka): Madam, I would like to draw the 
attention of the hon. Minister of Civil Aviation to the need for expediting the

The Bangalore International Airport at Devanahalli, to be built at a cost of US $ 
230 million {Rs. 11 SOcrores), would be India's first corporate, greenfield, airport, with 
strong international, private sector participation. Apart from teh equity brought 
in by the consortium of Siemens, L&T and Zurich Airport, foreign landers are 
also interested in financing the project. 
One major concern of foreign investors and lenders is the legislative framework 
withiii which the Airport Company would build, operate and maintain the Airport. 
Section 1 (3) of the Airports Authority of India Act, 1994 provides that all airports, 
irrespective of whether they are built and operated by AAl, or any toher authority, 
would come under the purview of the above Act. This increases the regulatory 
risk of the project, in the eyes of foreign investors and lenders. The Directors 
representing the consortium had called on the Chief Minister and, itner alia, 
emphasised the need for the amendment. 
Section 1(3) of the AAl Act, 1994 has, therefore, to be amended, to take away 
its applicability to airports that are not built and operated by AAl. The State 
Government has been playing a proactive role to get the amendments finalised. 
The legal advisors have already suggested the necessary draft amendments to 
the Ministry of Civil Aviation. 
The Ministry of Civil Aviation Is working towards obtaining the necessary 
approvals and introducing a Bill to amend Section 1(3) of the AAl Act int he 
current session of Parliament. 
1, once again, request the Minsiter of Civil Aviation to expedite the amendment 
to the Airports Authority of Idnia Act, 1994.   _

CLANDESTINE SUPPLY OF MISSILE TECHNOLOGY TO PAKISTAN BY 
NORTH KOREA 
SHR] RAJEEV SHUKLA (Uttar Pradesh): Madam, according to a recent 
newspaper column by a well-known journalist, a North Korean ship, carrying 
missile spares to Pakistan for its clandestine missile programme, was seized 
by the Coast Guard and Customs off Kandla Port in the summer of 2000. It 
was freed a few days later, after the captain pleaded that it was bound for Libya. 
The disquieting aspect is that Pakistan test-fired a few missiles, capable of 
carrying nuclear warheads, last month. By all accounts, it received the 
technology from North Korea. Notably, Pyongyang recently admitted to its 
nuclear capability, the technology for which, obviously, canie from Islamabad. 
It is a clear case of quid pro quo—Korea's missile technology for Pakistan's 
nuclear knowhow. It is apparent that the Korean ship's actual destination was 
Pakistan, and not Libya. 
Had the authorities acted with imagination, we could have prevented Pakistan 
from getting missile technology on the sly. It also highlights the need for toning up 
our intelligence agencies, including its external wing RAW, and better 
coordination between them and other authorities like the Coast Guard, the 
Customs and the Police. 
The Government should initiate a thorough probe into the whole episode and 
come out with a statement.
